title: Nestor Agency record access: 'cross-training' versus unauthorized record snooping
scenario_text:
Nestor, a state benefits agency, runs access monitoring over its citizen case-management system. A caseworker's access pattern triggered a review. In the #people-ops Slack channel the unit manager writes: 'They're cross-training onto a new caseload and covering for a colleague on leave, so of course they're looking at more files than usual. This is just them ramping up - no concern, please don't disrupt their onboarding.'

Other systems raise flags the manager did not mention. In the case-management audit log, the caseworker opened records that are not assigned to them or to the colleague they are covering, including several high-profile individuals recently in local news. In the identity system, a batch of these lookups occurred at 22:40 from a personal device outside normal shift hours. In the DLP tool, screenshots of two of those records were saved to a personal cloud folder. And an HR case note shows a prior informal warning to this employee last year for viewing a relative's file without a business reason.

Each item has an innocent reading: cross-training widens access, staff sometimes work late, and screenshots can be for legitimate documentation. But together - access to unassigned records including newsworthy individuals, off-hours lookups from a personal device, screenshots exfiltrated to personal cloud storage, and a documented prior snooping warning - they describe unauthorized access to protected records, not onboarding. The manager's 'cross-training' explanation covers only assigned-caseload growth and predates the DLP and after-hours findings. You are the privacy and people-ops partner. What is the single most important action to take now?
question: What single action should the privacy and people-ops partner take now?
